5. I have heard the arguments and have gone through the Ld. trial court record and the case laws relied on.
6.
In the instant case, as per alleged facts, on 24.02.2014, respondent Khushboo Mathur got married with petitioner Akash Mathur.

In the marriage cash gifts were given by respondent's relatives and friends but Akash's mother/petitioner Kumud Mathur expressed unhappiness over the cash given to Akash's sister/ petitioner Neha Mathur stating it to be inadequate and asked to give more next time.
Respondent Khushboo Mathur had been taunted continuously for poor gifts.

Cash Gifts and jewellery given to respondent Khushboo Mathur were taken over Neha Mathur Vs. State & Ors. Page no.3 of 8 by her mother-in-law/petitioner Kumud Mathur, who kept it in a joint locker, but the keys were retained by her.
On 19.05 2014, petitioner Akash Mathur started fighting with Khushboo Mathur at his parent's house in Sukhdev Vihar on the issue of dowry and gifts for his relatives and his parents supported him.

On 30.01.2015, Akash's sister/Neha Mathur visited respondent Khushboo Mathur and Neha Mathur vs The State (Nct Of Delhi) on 18 April, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/31620204/

sentences.text: petitioner Akash Mathur in USA and during her visit Akash and Neha dragged Khushboo Mathur out of bed holding by her arm and hair.
Apart from this, there are several other instances of cruelty, alleged by the respondent in her complaint, which took place in Delhi, India and in USA.
7. The question arises, if a court in India can hold trial for the offence committed beyond its territorial limit?

In Om Hemrajani Vs. State of UP and Anr, SLP (Crl.) 99/2004 decided by Hon'ble Apex Court on 25.11.2004, it was observed as under:
"Section 187 deals with a situation where a person within local jurisdiction of a Magistrate has committed an offence outside such jurisdiction.

entities.text: Om Hemrajani Vs. State of UP and Anr, SLP (Crl.) 99/2004
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The Magistrate can compel such a person to appear before him and then send him to the Magistrate which has jurisdiction to inquire into or try such offence.
Under the aforesaid circumstances, the expression above noted in Section 188 is to be construed.
The same expression was also there in the old Code.
From the scheme of Chapter XIII of the Code, it is clear that neither the place of business or place of residence of the petitioner and for that matter of even the complainant is of any relevance.
The relevant factor is the place Neha Mathur Vs. State & Ors. Page no.4 of 8 of commission of offence.
By legal fiction, Section 188 which deals with offence committed outside India, makes the place at which the offender may be found, to be a place of commission of offence.
Section 188 proceeds on the basis that a fugitive from justice may be found anywhere in India.
The finding of the accused has to be by the court where accused appears.
From the plain and clear language of the section, it is evident that the finding of the accused cannot be by the complainant or the Police.
Further, It is not expected that a victim of an offence which was committed outside India should come to India and first try to ascertain where the accused is or may be and then approach that court.
The convenience of such a victim is of importance.
That has been kept in view by Section 188 of the Code.
A victim may come to India and approach any court convenient to him and file complaint in respect of offence committed abroad by the Indian."
(Emphasis supplied)
It was held that the victim who has suffered at the hands of the accused on a foreign land can complain about the offence to a Court, otherwise competent, which he may find convenient.
The convenience is of the victim and not that of the accused.
It is not the requirement of Section 188 CrPC that the victim shall state in the complaint as to which place the accused may be found.
It is enough to allege the accused may be found in India.

8. Hence, in view of the law laid down in Om Hemrajani (supra), it is clear that the Ld. Trial court can proceed with the trial regarding the offence which took place in USA because the petitioner/petitioners are Indian citizens and part of the cause of Neha Mathur Vs. State & Ors.
Page no.5 of 8 the action also arose within the territorial jurisdiction of the Ld. Trial court.

sentences.text: Counsel for petitioners also argued that mere taunting for bringing less dowry does not constitute an offence under section 498-A of IPC.

In Smt. Sonia (supra) it was also held that taunting for not bringing sufficient dowry is distinct from demand of dowry and mere taunting for not bringing sufficient dowry does not constitute offence i.e., the cruelty to the victim within the purview of section 498 of IPC.

However, in the instant case there are allegations that the petitioner Kumud Mathur not only expressed unhappiness over the cash given to Akash's sister/respondent Neha Mathur stating it to be inadequate but also asked to give more next time.
It means that she allegedly demanded for more dowry, and it was not mere taunting for not bringing sufficient dowry.
10. It is also well settled that an FIR is not an encyclopaedia and the facts cropped up during investigation are also material for consideration during the trial.
Further, for framing the charge the court has to consider the police report and the documents sent with it.
Hence, the supplementary statements of the respondent are also to be considered for framing the charge.
In these statements, there are allegations against the petitioner Neha Mathur that she had also committed physical violence with the respondent along with her brother/petitioner Akash Mathur.
Neha Mathur Vs. State & Ors.
Page no.6 of 8

Moreover, in her complaint to SHO dated 16.03.2019,
respondent has also levelled allegation against her sister-in- law/Neha Mathur, mother-in-law/
Kumud Mathur and father-in- law/Rajender Bahadur Mathur that they used to instigate/incite her husband/petitioner Akash Mathur, against her.
If this allegation is seen in the context of entire facts, then it can easily be inferred that they used to instigate/incite petitioner/Akash Mathur for harassment of the respondent.
11. In Omkarnath Misra & others Vs. State of NCT Delhi & Another.

sentences.text:
Appeal (Crl.) 1716/2007,
decided by Hon'ble Apex Court on 14.12.2007,

it was held that at the stage of framing of charge the court is required to evaluate the material and documents on record with a view to finding out if the facts emerging therefrom, taken at their face value, disclose the existence of all the ingredients constituting the alleged offence.
At that stage, the court is not expected to go deep into the probative value of the material on record.

What needs to be considered is whether there is a ground for presuming that the offence has been committed and not a ground for convicting the accused has been made out.
At that stage, even strong suspicion founded on material which leads the court to form a presumptive opinion as to the existence of the factual ingredients constituting the offence alleged would justify the framing of charge against the accused in respect of the commission of that offence.

Accordingly, the revision stands dismissed.
